opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the opportunity is quite large, and it comes from looking at what agentic workloads actually do. They're not just one big model answering one question. You have chains of inference calls, often across several models of different sizes, with tool use, retrieval, and a lot of back-and-forth where the output of one step feeds the next. So the thing you really care about is latency per token, and especially latency for the whole sequence, not just throughput on large batches.

GPUs were designed for throughput. They do great when you can batch many requests together, but at low batch sizes, which is what you get when an agent is waiting on its own previous answer, you're mostly bound by memory bandwidth. You spend your time moving weights from HBM onto the chip, and the compute units sit idle much of the time.

That's where a dataflow architecture, the kind we've been building with reconfigurable dataflow units at SambaNova, really helps. You can fuse the whole model, or large parts of it, into a single spatial pipeline so intermediate results stay on chip instead of going back and forth to memory. Combine that with a tiered memory system, with large on-chip SRAM, HBM, and then a big pool of DDR capacity, and you can keep many models resident at once and switch between them in milliseconds rather than seconds. For agents that call several specialized models or experts, that matters a lot.

Put together, I think you can get something like an order of magnitude improvement in tokens per second per user, and similar gains in energy efficiency, compared with conventional GPU-based systems. And that's not just a nice-to-have. When an agent has to make dozens of model calls to complete a task, a 10x speedup turns something that takes minutes into something that feels interactive. That changes which applications are practical. So I'd say custom hardware is really what will make agentic AI economically and experientially viable at scale.

r001.rationale: It says agentic workloads involve chains of inference calls across models, and emphasizes low latency for the whole sequence.

r002.rationale: It says the system can keep many models resident and switch between them in milliseconds rather than seconds.

r003.rationale: It estimates an order-of-magnitude improvement in tokens per second per user, with similar gains in energy efficiency—approximately a 10x performance-per-watt improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the way I think about agentic AI is that it changes the shape of the workload compared to what we've been optimizing for. With a chatbot, you have a human in the loop, and the human reads at maybe a few hundred tokens per minute, so latency that's fine for a person was fine for the system. With agents, there's no human reading the output. The model is generating tokens that feed into tool calls, that feed into other models, that get reasoned over, planned over, and the whole thing loops. So the latency of each step compounds. If one agent takes ten seconds to produce a response and you've chained together twenty or thirty of those steps, you're waiting minutes for a result that should take seconds. The latency becomes the limiting factor on what the agent can actually do.

And that's where custom hardware really matters. On GPUs, decode is fundamentally memory bandwidth bound. You're moving the weights from HBM into the compute for every token, and the arithmetic intensity is terrible at small batch sizes. So the way people get economics out of GPUs is to batch really aggressively, which is exactly the wrong thing for an agent that wants its individual request answered fast.

What we've done at SambaNova with the reconfigurable dataflow architecture is attack this at the memory system. We have a three-tier memory hierarchy, with on-chip SRAM, then HBM, and then a very large pool of DDR that can hold hundreds of billions or even trillions of parameters. That lets us keep many models resident at the same time and switch between them in microseconds instead of the hundreds of milliseconds it takes to swap weights in and out of a GPU. For agents, that's exactly the pattern you want, because a real agentic system isn't one model. It's a router, a planner, several specialized models, maybe a verifier, all being invoked in sequence.

So concretely, I think we're talking about an order of magnitude improvement in per-token latency, so hundreds to a thousand tokens per second on a frontier-scale model, and probably a similar improvement in cost per token at the batch sizes agents actually run at, because you're not paying for all that memory traffic. But the more interesting improvement isn't the raw number. It's that when inference gets ten times faster, you can afford to let the agent do ten times more reasoning, more search, more self-verification in the same wall-clock budget. The quality of what the agent produces goes up, not just the speed. That's the thing I find exciting. Hardware stops being a cost center and becomes the thing that determines how smart your agents can be.

r001.rationale: The response explains that agent workflows chain multiple model calls and tool steps, so each step’s latency compounds and makes low-latency inference important.

r002.rationale: It describes keeping many models resident and switching between them in microseconds, supporting the router, planner, specialized models, and verifier used by an agent.

r003.rationale: It estimates roughly tenfold improvements in per-token latency and cost per token, but does not estimate a 5-to-10-fold improvement in performance per watt.

astra-6.text:
I think the big opportunity is reducing latency. With agentic AI, you’re not just generating one response. You may have a sequence of model calls, tool calls, and reasoning steps, and the time for each of those adds up. If we can make the model execution substantially faster, that gives the agent room to do more work while still responding in a useful amount of time.

Custom hardware lets you design the memory system and the computation around that workload. The improvement depends on where the bottleneck is—you can’t accelerate a slow external tool simply by making the AI chip faster. But faster, more efficient inference can change how much reasoning and exploration you can afford to give an agent.

r001.rationale: The response says faster model execution can reduce latency and notes that agentic workflows involve multiple model calls. It does not clearly state that ultra-low-latency inference is required.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify fast switching between multiple models as a way to support agentic AI.

r003.rationale: The response gives no estimate of a 5-to-10-fold improvement in performance per watt.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is to make the entire agent workflow more efficient. An agent isn’t just generating one response—it may be reasoning, calling tools, retrieving information, and then coming back to the model repeatedly. So latency and the cost of moving data become very important.

Custom hardware lets you tailor the architecture to those workloads: keep more of the relevant data close to the compute, use the right numerical precision, and avoid some of the overhead of a general-purpose machine. That could let you do more reasoning within the same time and energy budget.

I’d be careful about putting one improvement number on agentic AI, though. It depends on where the bottleneck is. If the agent is waiting on an external tool, faster model execution won’t eliminate that wait. You have to look at the whole system.

r001.rationale: It says agents return to the model repeatedly and that latency matters, but it does not state that inference needs ultra-low latency.

r002.rationale: It does not mention switching quickly between multiple models.

r003.rationale: It gives no 5-to-10× performance-per-watt estimate and explicitly avoids giving one improvement number.
